I don't really know if I've lost interest, exactly. I just... I don't feel much of anything toward the things I used to care about. It's like my brain just isn't registering it. 

Which is weird, because I used to care so much about everything. Like my wardrobe, for example. I used to spend hours picking out outfits and making sure everything coordinated perfectly. I don't know if they *no longer* do, it's just... I'm not really tracking that sort of thing right now. Like, I don't sit down and think, "Am I enjoying this?" 

I used to do that, though, when I was choreographing more often. You have to be so hyper-aware of how a movement feels, how it translates to an audience. I saw this documentary about the hot springs there, and they look amazing, but apparently, they smell strongly of sulfur. Like rotten eggs. I don't know if I could relax in a pool that smells like breakfast gone wrong, you know? I mean, yeah, I guess I do. I feel totally wiped out after doing just small things. Like, I'll answer one email to a dancer about scheduling, or just take a shower with this stupid ankle brace on, and I'm exhausted. And lying down doesn't really recharge me, either.

I think so, yeah. It's like... even just crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels so slowed down. Like my body is moving through wet sand instead of music.

I mean, yeah, constantly. I keep replaying the cancelled performances in my head, over and over. I just keep telling myself I let everyone down—the dancers, the funders, the whole community. Even though people have actually been way kinder about it than I deserve.

The morning light coming through those big arched windows was just perfect. The studio is in this old converted warehouse downtown, right next to a place that roasts their own coffee beans. She had hired this professional photographer who brought all these huge umbrellas and lighting rigs right into our living room, and the guy kept tripping over the rug. It's this antique Persian rug my grandmother left us, and the edges are all frayed because her cat used to use it as a scratching post... \n\nBut um, no. No thoughts of hurting myself at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself fidgeting or having trouble sitting still?\n\nPatient: Well, sitting still isn't really the issue. It's actually the opposite right now. I just... I feel so heavy. Like, recently, even just crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels incredibly slowed down, like my body is moving through wet sand instead of music. \n\nWhich is so frustrating because I usually have this very specific notebook I use for choreography. It's this Moleskine one with dotted pages, not lined. I hate lined paper for notes, it feels too restrictive. I actually buy them in bulk from this little stationery store in my old neighborhood. He has this massive collection of vintage fountain pens displayed in a glass case by the register. He spent like three hours cleaning the dried ink out of the nib with this tiny little ultrasonic cleaner. It was fascinating, honestly. He showed me how the gold nibs flex differently depending on how much pressure you apply. My grandfather used to use a fountain pen. He had this beautiful cursive handwriting, the kind they don't teach in schools anymore. He used to write me these long letters when I was away at summer dance intensive in New York. The intensive was at this old building near Lincoln Center, and the elevators were always broken, so we had to walk up six flights of stairs every morning. By the time we got to the studio, we were already sweating. There was this one girl there, Chloe, who used to bring these elaborate bento box lunches her mom made... \n\nBut yeah, no fidgeting. She collects seashells. Her whole guest bathroom is ocean-themed, which is honestly a little tacky if you ask me, but she loves it. She even has this shower curtain with giant sea turtles on it. She found it at Target on clearance. Target always has the best clearance section, especially right after a holiday. They always taste better than the regular cups, I swear it's because the peanut butter to chocolate ratio is different. My old roommate used to put them in the freezer. She was obsessed with freezing all her candy, even gummy bears, which just makes them impossible to chew. The dry cleaner always smelled heavily of chemicals, like that really sharp PERC smell... \n\nBut yeah, to answer your question, everything just feels really slowed down right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're at a point where you can't imagine things getting better?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I guess so. It's just this constant feeling that nothing is ever going to change. \n\nI used to wake up so early, you know? Like 5:30 AM, before the sun was even up, just to get to the studio and stretch before anyone else got there. The morning light coming through those big arched windows was just perfect. The studio is in this old converted warehouse downtown, right next to a place that roasts their own coffee beans. The smell of the roasting coffee would drift in through the vents around 7 AM every day. It's this vintage velvet wingback chair I found at a flea market in Brooklyn like ten years ago. The guy selling it wanted two hundred dollars, but I talked him down to eighty because there was a small tear on the back. I bought like ten skeins of merino wool yarn thinking I was going to learn how to knit a sweater, but I only ever made a very lopsided scarf that I ended up giving to my niece. She's seven, so she didn't care that it was crooked. She just loved that it was bright purple. Her whole bedroom is purple, actually. Even the ceiling...\n\nBut, um, to answer your question, yeah. It reminds me of when we were trying to score this contemporary piece last spring, and the composer kept asking me to rate the intensity of the climax on a scale of one to ten. He was this brilliant guy, but very numbers-driven. He actually used to be an actuary before he went back to school for music composition. He said the risk assessment models he used for insurance companies actually helped him understand musical tension and release. He worked for this huge firm in Chicago, right in the Loop. My cousin lived in Chicago for a while, right off the blue line. She used to complain about the noise all the time, but I always thought the sound of the train was kind of rhythmic. Almost like a metronome. She had this tiny apartment with exposed brick walls that were always shedding red dust on her furniture. She had to buy this special HEPA vacuum cleaner just to keep up with it. It was one of those Dyson ones that looks like a spaceship. I always wanted a Dyson, but they're so expensive. I ended up getting a refurbished Shark on Amazon Prime Day instead. It works okay, but the cord is just slightly too short to reach the far corner of my living room, which drives me crazy because I have this large fiddle leaf fig tree there that drops dry leaves... \n\nBut yeah, I don't know if this is the worst it's ever been. It's just... really heavy right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you might be experiencing a major depressive episode?\n\nPatient: I mean, I don't really know what to call it. I'm not a doctor, you know? They hired this local sculptor to redesign the centerpiece, and he made this abstract bronze thing that looks kind of like a flock of birds taking off, or maybe a twisted up tree root. He ordered the same thing every day—a large black coffee and an almond croissant. The almond croissants there were amazing, they had this thick layer of marzipan inside. I tried making marzipan at home once for my mom's birthday cake. She loves anything with almonds. But it turned out super gritty because I didn't use the right kind of powdered sugar. I guess there's a difference between regular powdered sugar and the extra-fine kind they use in bakeries...\n\nBut anyway, to your question... I don't really know the medical term for what I'm going through. I just know it feels awful."
